newsitem.title: USA: Office Depot to increase openings after Staples deal nixed.
newsitem.headline: Office Depot to increase openings after Staples deal nixed.

text.p: Office Depot Inc. Chief Executive David Fuente said Tuesday his company's $4.6 billion deal to merge with Staples Inc. was dead and that Office Depot would resume its fast pace of expansion by 1998.

U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan Hogan, in a preliminary injuction, ruled Monday that the Federal Trade Commission had shown a "reasonable probability" the merger would substantially impair competition.
Fuente told Reuters that Office Depot would take a charge of $6 million or more in the second quarter to cover fees paid to lawyers and investment bankers arising from the thwarted merger.
Office Depot, a leading U.S. operator of office-goods superstores, took a similar $6 million charge against its first-quarter earnings.

Wall Street analysts have estimated Office Depot earned 21 cents a share in the just-ended second quarter before taking into account charges arising from the failed Staples merger agreed last September.
He said Office Depot's board of directors was scheduled to meet Wednesday but was unlikely to vote to appeal Monday's judicial ruling blocking the Staples deal.

The combination of rivals Staples and Office Depot would have created by far the biggest office-supply retailer in the country and was opposed on antitrust grounds by federal regulators and at least eight state governments.
According to analysts, the proposed merger has consumed top management's thinking since September and slowed Delray Beach, Fla.-based Office Depot's fast pace of store openings.

Alex Brown & Sons analyst Christopher Vroom said Office Depot had lost several key executives in its development operation since September and may be six months or more behind its plan for opening new stores.
"We would have liked to open 80 stores this year; we will do about 40," Fuente said. "I fully expect to return to our 80-to-100 rate in 1998."
Fuente said Office Depot's finances were sound and had not been hurt by the drawn-out struggle to merge but that rebuilding the company's development operation was a key short-term management task.
Office Depot has $50 million or more in cash and an untapped credit line of $350 million to finance store openings, he said.
Vroom said Office Depot was likely to expand in the Northeast, a stronghold of Staples, as well as in Southeastern and other markets not yet fully penetrated by the company.
But Fuente said only Philadelphia and Boston in the Northeast were attractive to Office Depot and he had no plans to open outlets there anytime soon.
Office Depot was most immediately interested in south Florida, Atlanta and smaller markets, he said.
Vroom said Office Depot would need three to six months to normalise its business.

Office Depot's stock fell $3.81 to $15.625 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most active issue. Staples rose $1.06 to $24.31 on Nasdaq, where it was the most heavily traded stock.
